blocks.text: • ✓ The artist (who) we met is famous. (we is the subject; who is the object → can be dropped)
blocks.html: • ✓ The artist (who) we met is famous. (we is the subject; who is the object → can be dropped)

blocks.text: • ✓ The phone (that) I bought is broken.
blocks.html: • ✓ The phone (that) I bought is broken.

blocks.text: Quick test: If a noun or pronoun (like I, she, they) comes straight after the relative word, that word is the object and can usually be left out (in defining clauses). If a verb comes straight after, it is the subject and must stay.
blocks.html: Quick test: If a noun or pronoun (like I, she, they) comes straight after the relative word, that word is the object and can usually be left out (in defining clauses). If a verb comes straight after, it is the subject and must stay.

blocks.text: Whose for Possession
blocks.html: Whose for Possession

blocks.text: Whose shows that something belongs to the antecedent. It works for both people and things and is always followed by a noun.
blocks.html: Whose shows that something belongs to the antecedent. It works for both people and things and is always followed by a noun.

blocks.text: • ✓ That’s the boy whose dog ran away.
blocks.html: • ✓ That’s the boy whose dog ran away.

blocks.text: • ✓ I work for a company whose products are sold worldwide. (a thing — company)
blocks.html: • ✓ I work for a company whose products are sold worldwide. (a thing — company)

blocks.text: • ✓ The author, whose first novel sold millions, lives nearby. (non-defining)
blocks.html: • ✓ The author, whose first novel sold millions, lives nearby. (non-defining)

blocks.text: Do not confuse whose (possession) with who’s (= who is / who has).
blocks.html: Do not confuse whose (possession) with who’s (= who is / who has).

blocks.text: • ✗ The man who’s car was stolen called the police.
blocks.html: • ✗ The man who’s car was stolen called the police.

blocks.text: • ✓ The man whose car was stolen called the police.
blocks.html: • ✓ The man whose car was stolen called the police.

blocks.text: Relative Adverbs: Where, When, Why
blocks.html: Relative Adverbs: Where, When, Why

blocks.text: These replace a preposition + which and sound more natural.
blocks.html: These replace a preposition + which and sound more natural.

blocks.text: • Place — where: ✓ This is the café where we first met. (= in which)
blocks.html: • Place — where: ✓ This is the café where we first met. (= in which)

blocks.text: • Time — when: ✓ I’ll never forget the year when I moved abroad. (= in which)
blocks.html: • Time — when: ✓ I’ll never forget the year when I moved abroad. (= in which)

blocks.text: • Reason — why: ✓ Tell me the reason why you’re upset. (= for which)
blocks.html: • Reason — why: ✓ Tell me the reason why you’re upset. (= for which)

blocks.text: With when and why in defining clauses, the adverb can often be dropped: the year (when) I moved, the reason (why) you’re upset. With where, dropping it changes the structure: the place where I live vs the place I live in.
blocks.html: With when and why in defining clauses, the adverb can often be dropped: the year (when) I moved, the reason (why) you’re upset. With where, dropping it changes the structure: the place where I live vs the place I live in.

blocks.text: Prepositions in Relative Clauses
blocks.html: Prepositions in Relative Clauses

blocks.text: When the relative clause contains a preposition, English offers two styles.
blocks.html: When the relative clause contains a preposition, English offers two styles.

blocks.text: Informal / everyday — the preposition stays at the end, and the pronoun is often dropped:
blocks.html: Informal / everyday — the preposition stays at the end, and the pronoun is often dropped:

blocks.text: • ✓ The man (who) I spoke to is the manager.
blocks.html: • ✓ The man (who) I spoke to is the manager.

blocks.text: • ✓ The house (that) we live in is old.
blocks.html: • ✓ The house (that) we live in is old.

blocks.text: Formal / written — the preposition moves to the front, before the pronoun. Here you must use whom (for people) or which (for things), and you can never use that or omit the pronoun:
blocks.html: Formal / written — the preposition moves to the front, before the pronoun. Here you must use whom (for people) or which (for things), and you can never use that or omit the pronoun:

blocks.text: • ✓ The man to whom I spoke is the manager.
blocks.html: • ✓ The man to whom I spoke is the manager.

blocks.text: • ✓ The house in which we live is old.
blocks.html: • ✓ The house in which we live is old.

blocks.text: • ✗ The man to who I spoke… — ✗ The house in that we live…
blocks.html: • ✗ The man to who I spoke… — ✗ The house in that we live…

blocks.text: British / American note: Both varieties accept end-position prepositions in speech, and both reserve front-position to whom / in which for formal contexts. The “rule” that you must never end a sentence with a preposition is a myth — the man I spoke to is perfectly correct English.
blocks.html: British / American note: Both varieties accept end-position prepositions in speech, and both reserve front-position to whom / in which for formal contexts. The “rule” that you must never end a sentence with a preposition is a myth — the man I spoke to is perfectly correct English.

blocks.text: Which Referring to a Whole Clause
blocks.html: Which Referring to a Whole Clause

blocks.text: In a non-defining clause, which can refer back not to a single noun but to the whole previous idea. A comma always comes before it.
blocks.html: In a non-defining clause, which can refer back not to a single noun but to the whole previous idea. A comma always comes before it.

blocks.text: • ✓ He arrived an hour late, which annoyed me. (which = the fact that he was late)
blocks.html: • ✓ He arrived an hour late, which annoyed me. (which = the fact that he was late)

blocks.text: • ✓ She offered to pay for everyone, which was very generous.
blocks.html: • ✓ She offered to pay for everyone, which was very generous.

blocks.text: • ✗ He arrived late, what annoyed me.
blocks.html: • ✗ He arrived late, what annoyed me.

blocks.text: Watch out: This use of which always needs a comma, and you can never replace it with what or that.
blocks.html: Watch out: This use of which always needs a comma, and you can never replace it with what or that.

blocks.text: Reduced Relative Clauses (Participle Clauses)
blocks.html: Reduced Relative Clauses (Participle Clauses)

blocks.text: You can often shorten a relative clause by removing the pronoun and the verb be, leaving a participle.
blocks.html: You can often shorten a relative clause by removing the pronoun and the verb be, leaving a participle.

blocks.text: Present participle (-ing) replaces an active clause:
blocks.html: Present participle (-ing) replaces an active clause:

blocks.text: • The man who is standing there → The man standing there
blocks.html: • The man who is standing there → The man standing there

blocks.text: • Passengers who are travelling to Rome → Passengers travelling to Rome
blocks.html: • Passengers who are travelling to Rome → Passengers travelling to Rome

blocks.text: Past participle (-ed / -en) replaces a passive clause:
blocks.html: Past participle (-ed / -en) replaces a passive clause:

blocks.text: • The letter which was written by hand → The letter written by hand
blocks.html: • The letter which was written by hand → The letter written by hand

blocks.text: • The cars that were damaged in the storm → The cars damaged in the storm
blocks.html: • The cars that were damaged in the storm → The cars damaged in the storm

blocks.text: These reduced forms are common in both writing and speech and make sentences more compact.
blocks.html: These reduced forms are common in both writing and speech and make sentences more compact.

blocks.text: Quantifier + of whom / of which
blocks.html: Quantifier + of whom / of which

blocks.text: In formal English, you can combine a quantifier (some, many, most, all, none, both, several) with of whom (people) or of which (things). This always forms a non-defining clause with commas.
blocks.html: In formal English, you can combine a quantifier (some, many, most, all, none, both, several) with of whom (people) or of which (things). This always forms a non-defining clause with commas.

blocks.text: • ✓ The team has twelve players, several of whom are injured.
blocks.html: • ✓ The team has twelve players, several of whom are injured.

blocks.text: • ✓ He gave me three reasons, none of which convinced me.
blocks.html: • ✓ He gave me three reasons, none of which convinced me.

blocks.text: • ✓ She owns two cars, both of which are electric.
blocks.html: • ✓ She owns two cars, both of which are electric.

blocks.text: Common Mistakes
blocks.html: Common Mistakes

blocks.text: Mistake 1 — using what instead of that / which. What is not a relative pronoun for nouns. ✗ The book what I read… → ✓ The book (that) I read…
blocks.html: Mistake 1 — using what instead of that / which. What is not a relative pronoun for nouns. ✗ The book what I read… → ✓ The book (that) I read…

blocks.text: Mistake 2 — commas with defining clauses. Essential information takes no commas. ✗ People, who smoke, risk their health. → ✓ People who smoke risk their health.
blocks.html: Mistake 2 — commas with defining clauses. Essential information takes no commas. ✗ People, who smoke, risk their health. → ✓ People who smoke risk their health.

blocks.text: Mistake 3 — that in a non-defining clause. Use who / which after a comma. ✗ Paris, that is in France, is beautiful. → ✓ Paris, which is in France, is beautiful.
blocks.html: Mistake 3 — that in a non-defining clause. Use who / which after a comma. ✗ Paris, that is in France, is beautiful. → ✓ Paris, which is in France, is beautiful.

blocks.text: Mistake 4 — the double subject. Do not repeat the subject with an extra pronoun. ✗ The man who he lives here is my uncle. → ✓ The man who lives here is my uncle. ✗ The book that I read it was good. → ✓ The book (that) I read was good.
blocks.html: Mistake 4 — the double subject. Do not repeat the subject with an extra pronoun. ✗ The man who he lives here is my uncle. → ✓ The man who lives here is my uncle. ✗ The book that I read it was good. → ✓ The book (that) I read was good.

blocks.text: Quick Review
blocks.html: Quick Review

blocks.text: • A relative clause describes a noun and is introduced by a relative pronoun (who, which, that, whose, whom) or adverb (where, when, why).
blocks.html: • A relative clause describes a noun and is introduced by a relative pronoun (who, which, that, whose, whom) or adverb (where, when, why).

blocks.text: • Defining clauses give essential information: no commas, that is allowed, and the object pronoun can be omitted.
blocks.html: • Defining clauses give essential information: no commas, that is allowed, and the object pronoun can be omitted.

blocks.text: • Non-defining clauses give extra information: commas required, no that, and the pronoun is never omitted.
blocks.html: • Non-defining clauses give extra information: commas required, no that, and the pronoun is never omitted.

blocks.text: • Subject pronouns (followed by a verb) cannot be dropped; object pronouns (followed by subject + verb) can be — but only in defining clauses.
blocks.html: • Subject pronouns (followed by a verb) cannot be dropped; object pronouns (followed by subject + verb) can be — but only in defining clauses.

blocks.text: • Whose shows possession for people and things; where / when / why replace in/at/for which.
blocks.html: • Whose shows possession for people and things; where / when / why replace in/at/for which.

blocks.text: • Prepositions go at the end informally (the man I spoke to) or at the front formally (the man to whom I spoke).
blocks.html: • Prepositions go at the end informally (the man I spoke to) or at the front formally (the man to whom I spoke).

blocks.text: • Which after a comma can refer to a whole clause: He was late, which annoyed me.
blocks.html: • Which after a comma can refer to a whole clause: He was late, which annoyed me.

blocks.text: • Reduced clauses use participles: the man standing there, the letter written by hand.
blocks.html: • Reduced clauses use participles: the man standing there, the letter written by hand.

blocks.text: Practice
blocks.html: Practice

blocks.text: Complete or correct each sentence.
blocks.html: Complete or correct each sentence.

blocks.text: 1. Fill the gap: The woman ____ won the race is my neighbour. (who / which)
blocks.html: 1. Fill the gap: The woman ____ won the race is my neighbour. (who / which)

blocks.text: 2. Fill the gap: This is the museum ____ the painting is kept. (where / which)
blocks.html: 2. Fill the gap: This is the museum ____ the painting is kept. (where / which)

blocks.text: 3. Add commas if needed: My grandmother who is eighty-five still drives. (assume only one grandmother)
blocks.html: 3. Add commas if needed: My grandmother who is eighty-five still drives. (assume only one grandmother)

blocks.text: 4. Can the pronoun be omitted? The film that was released yesterday is a hit. (yes / no — why?)
blocks.html: 4. Can the pronoun be omitted? The film that was released yesterday is a hit. (yes / no — why?)

blocks.text: 5. Correct the error: The boy what broke the window ran away.
blocks.html: 5. Correct the error: The boy what broke the window ran away.

blocks.text: 6. Correct the error: London, that is the capital of England, is huge.
blocks.html: 6. Correct the error: London, that is the capital of England, is huge.

blocks.text: 7. Make it formal (front-position preposition): The colleague who I work with is helpful.
blocks.html: 7. Make it formal (front-position preposition): The colleague who I work with is helpful.

blocks.text: 8. Combine using which (referring to the whole idea): She passed all her exams. This made her parents proud.
blocks.html: 8. Combine using which (referring to the whole idea): She passed all her exams. This made her parents proud.

blocks.text: 9. Reduce the clause to a participle: The students who are waiting outside can come in now.
blocks.html: 9. Reduce the clause to a participle: The students who are waiting outside can come in now.

blocks.text: 10. Correct the error: The man who he called me was very polite.
blocks.html: 10. Correct the error: The man who he called me was very polite.

blocks.text: Answers
blocks.html: Answers

blocks.text: 1. who — who refers to a person (the woman).
blocks.html: 1. who — who refers to a person (the woman).

blocks.text: 2. where — it refers to a place (the museum).
blocks.html: 2. where — it refers to a place (the museum).

blocks.text: 3. My grandmother, who is eighty-five, still drives. — With only one grandmother, the clause is non-defining, so commas are needed.
blocks.html: 3. My grandmother, who is eighty-five, still drives. — With only one grandmother, the clause is non-defining, so commas are needed.

blocks.text: 4. No. That is the subject of the clause (followed by the verb was released); subject pronouns can never be omitted.
blocks.html: 4. No. That is the subject of the clause (followed by the verb was released); subject pronouns can never be omitted.

blocks.text: 5. The boy who / that broke the window ran away. — What cannot be used as a relative pronoun here.
blocks.html: 5. The boy who / that broke the window ran away. — What cannot be used as a relative pronoun here.

blocks.text: 6. London, which is the capital of England, is huge. — That is not allowed in a non-defining (comma) clause.
blocks.html: 6. London, which is the capital of England, is huge. — That is not allowed in a non-defining (comma) clause.

blocks.text: 7. The colleague with whom I work is helpful.
blocks.html: 7. The colleague with whom I work is helpful.

blocks.text: 8. She passed all her exams, which made her parents proud.
blocks.html: 8. She passed all her exams, which made her parents proud.

blocks.text: 9. The students waiting outside can come in now.
blocks.html: 9. The students waiting outside can come in now.

blocks.text: 10. The man who called me was very polite. — Remove the double subject he.

chapters.title: Questions, Negatives & Question Tags
chapters.text:
Chapter 24 — Questions, Negatives & Question Tags

Questions and negatives are the engines of conversation. Every time you ask for directions, disagree politely, or check that someone is listening, you reach for the patterns in this chapter. The good news is that English builds nearly all of them from one simple idea: the auxiliary verb (a helping verb such as do, be, have, or a modal like can) carries the grammatical work, while the main verb stays calm and unchanged. Master the auxiliary, and questions, negatives, short answers, and question tags all fall into place.

Let’s build them up step by step.

Forming Negatives

To make a sentence negative, we add not (or its contraction n’t) after an auxiliary verb or after the verb be.

With be and auxiliary verbs

When the sentence already contains be, a modal, or a perfect/continuous auxiliary, simply add not / n’t after it. No extra word is needed.

• ✓ She is not (isn’t) ready.

• ✓ They are not (aren’t) coming.

• ✓ I have not (haven’t) finished.

• ✓ He can not (cannot / can’t) swim.

• ✓ We will not (won’t) be late.

Present and past simple: do / does / did + not

The present simple and past simple have no auxiliary of their own, so we borrow do. This is called do-support. The borrowed do carries the tense and the person, and the main verb returns to its base form.

• ✓ I don’t like coffee. (not ✗ I don’t likes coffee.)

• ✓ She doesn’t work here. (not ✗ She doesn’t works.)

• ✓ They didn’t call. (not ✗ They didn’t called.)

Watch out — the verb loses its ending. Because does and did already show person and tense, the main verb stays in its base form: ✗ He doesn’t likes it. → ✓ He doesn’t like it. / ✗ We didn’t went. → ✓ We didn’t go.

Negatives of modal verbs

Modals form negatives directly with not / n’t. Note a few spellings:

Modal · Negative · Contraction
▸ can
   Negative: cannot
   Contraction: can’t
▸ could
   Negative: could not
   Contraction: couldn’t
▸ will
   Negative: will not
   Contraction: won’t
▸ would
   Negative: would not
   Contraction: wouldn’t
▸ should
   Negative: should not
   Contraction: shouldn’t
▸ must
   Negative: must not
   Contraction: mustn’t
▸ might
   Negative: might not
   Contraction: (mightn’t, rare)

• ✓ You mustn’t touch that.

• ✓ I won’t tell anyone.

Negatives with no and any

There are two natural ways to say you lack something:

• ✓ I don’t have any money. (negative verb + any)

• ✓ I have no money. (positive verb + no)

Both are correct and mean the same thing. The key rule: use any with a negative verb, and no with a positive verb. Do not combine two negatives.

Avoid the double negative. In standard English, one negative word per clause is enough. ✗ I don’t know nothing. → ✓ I don’t know anything. / ✓ I know nothing. Two negatives logically cancel out, so ✗ I didn’t see nobody literally means you did see somebody. (You may hear double negatives in songs and dialects, but avoid them in standard writing and speech.)

Yes/No Questions

A yes/no question can be answered with yes or no. We form it by putting the auxiliary or be in front of the subject. This swap is called inversion.

• ✓ Is she ready? (She is ready. → Is she ready?)

• ✓ Are they coming?

• ✓ Have you finished?

• ✓ Can he swim?

For the present and past simple, there is no auxiliary to move, so again we use do-support: place do / does / did before the subject and keep the main verb in its base form.

• ✓ Do you like coffee?

• ✓ Does she work here?

• ✓ Did they call?

A rising voice is not a question (in standard English). Saying ✗ You like coffee? with a question intonation happens in casual speech, but the standard, correct form uses inversion or do: ✓ Do you like coffee? Teach and write the inverted form.

Yes/No question forms across tenses

Tense · Statement · Yes/No question
▸ Present simple
   Statement: You work here.
   Yes/No question: Do you work here?
▸ Present simple (be)
   Statement: She is busy.
   Yes/No question: Is she busy?
▸ Present continuous
   Statement: They are eating.
   Yes/No question: Are they eating?
▸ Past simple
   Statement: He called.
   Yes/No question: Did he call?
▸ Past continuous
   Statement: You were sleeping.
   Yes/No question: Were you sleeping?
▸ Present perfect
   Statement: We have met.
   Yes/No question: Have we met?
▸ Past perfect
   Statement: She had left.
   Yes/No question: Had she left?
▸ Future (will)
   Statement: They will help.
   Yes/No question: Will they help?
▸ Modal
   Statement: He can drive.
   Yes/No question: Can he drive?

Wh- Questions

Wh- questions ask for information, not just yes or no. They begin with a question word, followed by the same inversion (or do-support) as a yes/no question:

Wh- word + auxiliary + subject + main verb

The main question words are who, what, which, whose, where, when, why, how, plus the how family: how much, how many, how long, how often, how old.

Question word · Asks about · Example
▸ who
   Asks about: a person
   Example: Who did you meet?
▸ what
   Asks about: a thing/idea
   Example: What do you want?
▸ which
   Asks about: a choice
   Example: Which do you prefer?
▸ whose
   Asks about: possession
   Example: Whose car is this?
▸ where
   Asks about: a place
   Example: Where did she go?
▸ when
   Asks about: a time
   Example: When does it start?
▸ why
   Asks about: a reason
   Example: Why are you laughing?
▸ how
   Asks about: a manner
   Example: How did they win?
▸ how much
   Asks about: quantity (uncountable)
   Example: How much does it cost?
▸ how many
   Asks about: quantity (countable)
   Example: How many do you need?
▸ how long
   Asks about: duration
   Example: How long have you waited?
▸ how often
   Asks about: frequency
   Example: How often do you exercise?
▸ how old
   Asks about: age
   Example: How old is your sister?

Subject vs Object Questions

This is one of the most important — and most misunderstood — points in English questions.

When the wh- word asks about the object of the verb, we use normal inversion / do-support:

• ✓ Who did you see? (you is the subject; who is the object)

• ✓ What did she break?

But when the wh- word is itself the subject of the verb, there is no inversion and no do/does/did. The question word simply takes the subject’s place, and the verb is conjugated normally.

• ✓ Who broke the window? (not ✗ Who did break the window?)

• ✓ What happened? (not ✗ What did happen?)

Subject questions take NO do/does/did. Compare these carefully: - Subject: ✓ Who wants ice cream? — Object: ✓ Who do you want? - Subject: ✓ What made that noise? — Object: ✓ What did you make? - Subject: ✓ Who called you? — Object: ✓ Who did you call? Ask yourself: who or what is doing the verb? If the wh- word is the doer, it is a subject question — keep it simple, no do.

Questions with Prepositions

In everyday English, prepositions usually stay at the end of the question, with the wh- word at the front:

• ✓ What are you looking at?

• ✓ Who did you go with?

• ✓ Where does she come from?

• ✓ What is the meeting about?

In very formal English, the preposition can move to the front: With whom did you go? This sounds stiff and old-fashioned in conversation, so prefer the end position for natural speech and most writing.

Indirect / Embedded Questions

When we put a question inside another sentence — often to be more polite — the word order changes back to that of a statement. There is no inversion and no do/does/did.

Direct question · Indirect / embedded question
▸ Where is the station? — Could you tell me where the station is?
▸ What does it mean? — I don’t know what it means.
▸ When did they leave? — Do you remember when they left?

• ✓ Could you tell me where the station is? (not ✗ …where is the station?)

• ✓ I wonder why she didn’t call. (not ✗ …why didn’t she call.)

For yes/no questions embedded in a sentence, use if or whether:

• ✓ I wonder if it will rain.

• ✓ Do you know whether the shop is open?

Indirect questions use statement order. The most common mistake is keeping the inverted order: ✗ Can you tell me what time is it? → ✓ Can you tell me what time it is? Embedded questions sound much more polite, which is why we use them to ask strangers for help.

Negative Questions

A negative question puts not / n’t into the question. We use them to express surprise, or to invite the listener to agree with us.

• Don’t you like it? (surprise: I expected you to like it)

• Isn’t this beautiful? (inviting agreement)

• Haven’t we met before? (seeking confirmation)

Answering negative questions can be tricky for learners. In English, base your yes or no on the facts, not on the wording of the question:

• Don’t you like coffee? — ✓ Yes, I do. (= I do like it) / ✓ No, I don’t. (= I don’t like it)

So yes always goes with a positive fact, and no always goes with a negative fact, regardless of how the question was phrased.

Short Answers and Short Responses

We rarely answer with a bare yes or no. Instead, we echo the auxiliary. Use the auxiliary or be from the question — never the full verb.

• Do you like it? — ✓ Yes, I do. / No, I don’t.

• Is she coming? — ✓ Yes, she is. / No, she isn’t.

• Can you drive? — ✓ Yes, I can. / No, I can’t.

• Have they arrived? — ✓ Yes, they have. / No, they haven’t.

Don’t repeat the main verb in a short answer. ✗ Do you like it? — Yes, I like. → ✓ Yes, I do. The auxiliary does all the work.

Question Tags

A question tag is a short question added to the end of a statement to check information or invite agreement: It’s cold today, isn’t it?

The rule has three parts:

1. Positive statement → negative tag; negative statement → positive tag.

2. Use the same auxiliary (or be) as the statement. If the statement is present/past simple with no auxiliary, use do / does / did.

3. Use a pronoun that matches the subject.

• ✓ She is tired, isn’t she? (positive → negative)

• ✓ She isn’t tired, is she? (negative → positive)

• ✓ You like tea, don’t you? (no auxiliary → do)

• ✓ He went home, didn’t he?

Question tags across tenses

Statement · Tag
▸ You’re a teacher, — aren’t you?
▸ She isn’t here, — is she?
▸ They live nearby, — don’t they?
▸ He doesn’t smoke, — does he?
▸ We met before, — didn’t we?
▸ You can swim, — can’t you?
▸ It won’t rain, — will it?
▸ She has left, — hasn’t she?
▸ You wouldn’t lie, — would you?

Special cases

A few tags do not follow the basic pattern and must be learned:

Statement · Tag · Note
▸ I’m late,
   Tag: aren’t I?
   Note: am I not is too formal; we say aren’t I
▸ Open the window,
   Tag: will you / won’t you / can you?
   Note: imperatives

Statement · Tag · Note
▸ Don’t be late,
   Tag: will you?
   Note: negative imperative
▸ Let’s go,
   Tag: shall we?
   Note: suggestions with let’s
▸ There’s a problem,
   Tag: isn’t there?
   Note: there repeats as the subject
▸ Everyone agrees,
   Tag: don’t they?
   Note: everyone / someone / nobody → they
▸ Nobody called,
   Tag: did they?
   Note: nobody is already negative → positive tag

Intonation changes the meaning. A falling voice on the tag means you expect agreement — you are not really asking: Lovely day, isn’t it?↓ A rising voice turns it into a genuine question: You locked the door, didn’t you?↑ (you truly want to know).

So / Neither + Auxiliary + Subject

To say that something is also true for someone, use so + auxiliary + subject (for positive statements) or neither / nor + auxiliary + subject (for negative statements). Notice the inversion — the auxiliary comes before the subject.

• I like jazz. — ✓ So do I. (= I like it too)

• She’s tired. — ✓ So am I.

• I can’t swim. — ✓ Neither can I. / ✓ Nor can I.

• He doesn’t eat meat. — ✓ Neither do I.

Match the auxiliary, and invert. ✗ So I do. → ✓ So do I. For negatives, do not add a second not: ✗ Neither I don’t. → ✓ Neither do I. (neither already carries the negative meaning).

Quick Review

• Negatives, questions, short answers, and tags all run on the auxiliary verb. For the present/past simple, borrow do/does/did and keep the main verb in its base form.

• Yes/no questions invert subject and auxiliary; wh- questions add a question word in front.

• Subject questions (Who broke it?) take no do/does/did and no inversion — this is the key trap.

• Indirect questions use statement word order and are more polite (Could you tell me where it is?).

• Avoid double negatives: use any with a negative verb, no with a positive verb.

• Question tags: opposite polarity, same auxiliary, pronoun subject — with special cases (aren’t I?, shall we?, isn’t there?).

• Use So do I / Neither do I to agree, matching the auxiliary and inverting.

Practice

Rewrite or complete each item correctly.

1. Make negative: She understands the question.

2. Make a yes/no question: They have finished the project.

3. Correct the error: He doesn’t likes vegetables.

4. Subject or object question? Complete: ______ wrote this letter? (the writer is unknown)

5. Make a wh- question asking about the object: You called ______ last night? → (use who)

6. Turn into an indirect question: Where is the bank? → Could you tell me ______?

7. Add a question tag: You’re coming to the party, ______?

8. Add a question tag: Let’s leave early, ______?

9. Correct the double negative: I didn’t see nobody.

10. Respond showing you agree: “I don’t like horror films.” “______ I.”

Answers

1. She doesn’t understand the question. (base form understand)

2. Have they finished the project?

3. He doesn’t like vegetables. (base form after doesn’t)

4. Who wrote this letter? — a subject question, so no do/did.

5. Who did you call last night? — an object question, so use did + base form.

6. Could you tell me where the bank is? (statement order, no inversion)

7. You’re coming to the party, aren’t you?

8. Let’s leave early, shall we?

9. I didn’t see anybody. (or I saw nobody.)

10. “Neither do I.” (or “Nor do I.”)

blocks.text: Questions and negatives are the engines of conversation. Every time you ask for directions, disagree politely, or check that someone is listening, you reach for the patterns in this chapter. The good news is that English builds nearly all of them from one simple idea: the auxiliary verb (a helping verb such as do, be, have, or a modal like can) carries the grammatical work, while the main verb stays calm and unchanged. Master the auxiliary, and questions, negatives, short answers, and question tags all fall into place.

blocks.text: To make a sentence negative, we add not (or its contraction n’t) after an auxiliary verb or after the verb be.

blocks.html: With be and auxiliary verbs

blocks.text: When the sentence already contains be, a modal, or a perfect/continuous auxiliary, simply add not / n’t after it. No extra word is needed.

blocks.text: The present simple and past simple have no auxiliary of their own, so we borrow do. This is called do-support. The borrowed do carries the tense and the person, and the main verb returns to its base form.

blocks.html: • ✓ They didn’t call. (not ✗ They didn’t called.)

blocks.text: Watch out — the verb loses its ending. Because does and did already show person and tense, the main verb stays in its base form: ✗ He doesn’t likes it. → ✓ He doesn’t like it. / ✗ We didn’t went. → ✓ We didn’t go.

blocks.text: Negatives with no and any

blocks.text: There are two natural ways to say you lack something:
blocks.html: There are two natural ways to say you lack something:

blocks.text: • ✓ I don’t have any money. (negative verb + any)
blocks.html: • ✓ I don’t have any money. (negative verb + any)

blocks.text: • ✓ I have no money. (positive verb + no)

blocks.text: Both are correct and mean the same thing. The key rule: use any with a negative verb, and no with a positive verb. Do not combine two negatives.

blocks.text: Avoid the double negative. In standard English, one negative word per clause is enough. ✗ I don’t know nothing. → ✓ I don’t know anything. / ✓ I know nothing. Two negatives logically cancel out, so ✗ I didn’t see nobody literally means you did see somebody. (You may hear double negatives in songs and dialects, but avoid them in standard writing and speech.)

blocks.html: Yes/No Questions

blocks.text: A yes/no question can be answered with yes or no. We form it by putting the auxiliary or be in front of the subject. This swap is called inversion.

blocks.html: • ✓ Can he swim?

blocks.text: Wh- Questions
blocks.html: Wh- Questions

blocks.text: Wh- questions ask for information, not just yes or no. They begin with a question word, followed by the same inversion (or do-support) as a yes/no question:

blocks.text: Wh- word + auxiliary + subject + main verb
blocks.html: Wh- word + auxiliary + subject + main verb

blocks.text: The main question words are who, what, which, whose, where, when, why, how, plus the how family: how much, how many, how long, how often, how old.
blocks.html: The main question words are who, what, which, whose, where, when, why, how, plus the how family: how much, how many, how long, how often, how old.

▸ whose
   Asks about: possession
   Example: Whose car is this?
▸ where
   Asks about: a place
   Example: Where did she go?
▸ when
   Asks about: a time
   Example: When does it start?
▸ why
   Asks about: a reason
   Example: Why are you laughing?

   Example: How much does it cost?

   Example: How many do you need?

blocks.text: Subject vs Object Questions
blocks.html: Subject vs Object Questions

blocks.text: This is one of the most important — and most misunderstood — points in English questions.
blocks.html: This is one of the most important — and most misunderstood — points in English questions.

blocks.text: When the wh- word asks about the object of the verb, we use normal inversion / do-support:
blocks.html: When the wh- word asks about the object of the verb, we use normal inversion / do-support:

blocks.text: • ✓ Who did you see? (you is the subject; who is the object)
blocks.html: • ✓ Who did you see? (you is the subject; who is the object)

blocks.text: • ✓ What did she break?
blocks.html: • ✓ What did she break?

blocks.text: But when the wh- word is itself the subject of the verb, there is no inversion and no do/does/did. The question word simply takes the subject’s place, and the verb is conjugated normally.
blocks.html: But when the wh- word is itself the subject of the verb, there is no inversion and no do/does/did. The question word simply takes the subject’s place, and the verb is conjugated normally.

blocks.text: • ✓ Who broke the window? (not ✗ Who did break the window?)
blocks.html: • ✓ Who broke the window? (not ✗ Who did break the window?)

blocks.text: • ✓ What happened? (not ✗ What did happen?)
blocks.html: • ✓ What happened? (not ✗ What did happen?)

blocks.text: Subject questions take NO do/does/did. Compare these carefully: - Subject: ✓ Who wants ice cream? — Object: ✓ Who do you want? - Subject: ✓ What made that noise? — Object: ✓ What did you make? - Subject: ✓ Who called you? — Object: ✓ Who did you call? Ask yourself: who or what is doing the verb? If the wh- word is the doer, it is a subject question — keep it simple, no do.

Ask yourself: who or what is doing the verb? If the wh- word is the doer, it is a subject question — keep it simple, no do.

blocks.text: Questions with Prepositions
blocks.html: Questions with Prepositions

blocks.text: In everyday English, prepositions usually stay at the end of the question, with the wh- word at the front:
blocks.html: In everyday English, prepositions usually stay at the end of the question, with the wh- word at the front:

blocks.text: • ✓ What are you looking at?
blocks.html: • ✓ What are you looking at?

blocks.text: • ✓ Who did you go with?
blocks.html: • ✓ Who did you go with?

blocks.text: • ✓ Where does she come from?
blocks.html: • ✓ Where does she come from?

blocks.text: • ✓ What is the meeting about?
blocks.html: • ✓ What is the meeting about?

blocks.text: In very formal English, the preposition can move to the front: With whom did you go? This sounds stiff and old-fashioned in conversation, so prefer the end position for natural speech and most writing.

blocks.text: Indirect / Embedded Questions
blocks.html: Indirect / Embedded Questions

blocks.text: When we put a question inside another sentence — often to be more polite — the word order changes back to that of a statement. There is no inversion and no do/does/did.
blocks.html: When we put a question inside another sentence — often to be more polite — the word order changes back to that of a statement. There is no inversion and no do/does/did.

blocks.text:
Direct question · Indirect / embedded question
▸ Where is the station? — Could you tell me where the station is?
▸ What does it mean? — I don’t know what it means.
▸ When did they leave? — Do you remember when they left?

blocks.text: • ✓ Could you tell me where the station is? (not ✗ …where is the station?)
blocks.html: • ✓ Could you tell me where the station is? (not ✗ …where is the station?)

blocks.text: • ✓ I wonder why she didn’t call. (not ✗ …why didn’t she call.)
blocks.html: • ✓ I wonder why she didn’t call. (not ✗ …why didn’t she call.)

blocks.text: For yes/no questions embedded in a sentence, use if or whether:
blocks.html: For yes/no questions embedded in a sentence, use if or whether:

blocks.text: • ✓ I wonder if it will rain.
blocks.html: • ✓ I wonder if it will rain.

blocks.text: • ✓ Do you know whether the shop is open?
blocks.html: • ✓ Do you know whether the shop is open?

blocks.text: Indirect questions use statement order. The most common mistake is keeping the inverted order: ✗ Can you tell me what time is it? → ✓ Can you tell me what time it is? Embedded questions sound much more polite, which is why we use them to ask strangers for help.

blocks.text: Negative Questions
blocks.html: Negative Questions

blocks.text: A negative question puts not / n’t into the question. We use them to express surprise, or to invite the listener to agree with us.
blocks.html: A negative question puts not / n’t into the question. We use them to express surprise, or to invite the listener to agree with us.

blocks.text: • Don’t you like it? (surprise: I expected you to like it)
blocks.html: • Don’t you like it? (surprise: I expected you to like it)

blocks.text: • Isn’t this beautiful? (inviting agreement)
blocks.html: • Isn’t this beautiful? (inviting agreement)

blocks.text: • Haven’t we met before? (seeking confirmation)
blocks.html: • Haven’t we met before? (seeking confirmation)

blocks.text: Answering negative questions can be tricky for learners. In English, base your yes or no on the facts, not on the wording of the question:
blocks.html: Answering negative questions can be tricky for learners. In English, base your yes or no on the facts, not on the wording of the question:

blocks.text: • Don’t you like coffee? — ✓ Yes, I do. (= I do like it) / ✓ No, I don’t. (= I don’t like it)
blocks.html: • Don’t you like coffee? — ✓ Yes, I do. (= I do like it) / ✓ No, I don’t. (= I don’t like it)

blocks.text: So yes always goes with a positive fact, and no always goes with a negative fact, regardless of how the question was phrased.
blocks.html: So yes always goes with a positive fact, and no always goes with a negative fact, regardless of how the question was phrased.

blocks.text: Short Answers and Short Responses
blocks.html: Short Answers and Short Responses

blocks.text: We rarely answer with a bare yes or no. Instead, we echo the auxiliary. Use the auxiliary or be from the question — never the full verb.
blocks.html: We rarely answer with a bare yes or no. Instead, we echo the auxiliary. Use the auxiliary or be from the question — never the full verb.

blocks.text: • Do you like it? — ✓ Yes, I do. / No, I don’t.
blocks.html: • Do you like it? — ✓ Yes, I do. / No, I don’t.

blocks.text: • Is she coming? — ✓ Yes, she is. / No, she isn’t.
blocks.html: • Is she coming? — ✓ Yes, she is. / No, she isn’t.

blocks.text: • Can you drive? — ✓ Yes, I can. / No, I can’t.
blocks.html: • Can you drive? — ✓ Yes, I can. / No, I can’t.

blocks.text: • Have they arrived? — ✓ Yes, they have. / No, they haven’t.
blocks.html: • Have they arrived? — ✓ Yes, they have. / No, they haven’t.

blocks.text: Don’t repeat the main verb in a short answer. ✗ Do you like it? — Yes, I like. → ✓ Yes, I do. The auxiliary does all the work.

blocks.text: Question Tags
blocks.html: Question Tags

blocks.text: A question tag is a short question added to the end of a statement to check information or invite agreement: It’s cold today, isn’t it?
blocks.html: A question tag is a short question added to the end of a statement to check information or invite agreement: It’s cold today, isn’t it?

blocks.text: The rule has three parts:
blocks.html: The rule has three parts:

blocks.text: 1. Positive statement → negative tag; negative statement → positive tag.
blocks.html: 1. Positive statement → negative tag; negative statement → positive tag.

blocks.text: 2. Use the same auxiliary (or be) as the statement. If the statement is present/past simple with no auxiliary, use do / does / did.
blocks.html: 2. Use the same auxiliary (or be) as the statement. If the statement is present/past simple with no auxiliary, use do / does / did.

blocks.text: 3. Use a pronoun that matches the subject.
blocks.html: 3. Use a pronoun that matches the subject.

blocks.html: • ✓ She is tired, isn’t she? (positive → negative)

blocks.text: • ✓ She isn’t tired, is she? (negative → positive)
blocks.html: • ✓ She isn’t tired, is she? (negative → positive)

blocks.text: • ✓ You like tea, don’t you? (no auxiliary → do)
blocks.html: • ✓ You like tea, don’t you? (no auxiliary → do)

blocks.text: • ✓ He went home, didn’t he?
blocks.html: • ✓ He went home, didn’t he?

blocks.text: So / Neither + Auxiliary + Subject
blocks.html: So / Neither + Auxiliary + Subject

blocks.text: To say that something is also true for someone, use so + auxiliary + subject (for positive statements) or neither / nor + auxiliary + subject (for negative statements). Notice the inversion — the auxiliary comes before the subject.

blocks.text: • I like jazz. — ✓ So do I. (= I like it too)

chapters.title: Punctuation, Capitalization & Common Mistakes
chapters.text:
Chapter 25 — Punctuation, Capitalization & Common Mistakes

Punctuation and capitalization are the traffic signals of writing. They tell your reader when to pause, when to stop, where one idea ends and another begins, and which words deserve special weight. Get them right and your meaning flows clearly; get them wrong and even good ideas can confuse. This capstone chapter brings together the marks you will use every day, the capitalization rules that catch out even confident writers, and a practical reference to the mistakes and confused words that appear most often. Where British (BrE) and American (AmE) usage differ, we will say so clearly.

Part A — Punctuation

The Full Stop / Period, Question Mark, and Exclamation Mark

These three marks end sentences.

The full stop (BrE) or period (AmE) closes a statement or a command.

• ✓ She lives in Lisbon.

• ✓ Please close the door.

The question mark closes a direct question. Do not use it after an indirect (reported) question.

• ✓ Where do you live?

• ✗ I asked where she lived? → ✓ I asked where she lived.

The exclamation mark signals strong feeling, surprise, or emphasis. Use it sparingly; one is almost always enough.

• ✓ What a beautiful view!

• ✗ Thank you so much!!! → ✓ Thank you so much!

Tip: In formal writing, exclamation marks are rare. If everything is emphasized, nothing is.

The Comma — The Big One

The comma is the most useful and the most misused mark in English. It separates parts of a sentence so readers can group ideas correctly. Here are its main jobs.

1. Separating items in a list. Use commas between three or more items.

• ✓ We bought bread, cheese, and olives.

The comma before and (or or) in a list is called the serial comma or Oxford comma. It is standard in much American writing and optional in British writing. It can prevent ambiguity.

• ✓ I’d like to thank my parents, Oprah, and God. (three separate things)

• ✗ I’d like to thank my parents, Oprah and God. (could suggest your parents are Oprah and God)

BrE vs AmE — the Oxford comma: AmE often uses it by default; BrE often omits it unless needed for clarity. Either is acceptable — just be consistent within a piece of writing.

2. After an introductory element. Use a comma after an introductory word, phrase, or clause.

• ✓ After the meeting, we went for coffee.

• ✓ Honestly, I had no idea.

• ✓ Because it was raining, the match was cancelled.

3. Around non-essential information. If a phrase or clause adds extra (removable) detail, surround it with commas. If it is essential to the meaning, do not.

• ✓ My brother, who lives in Tokyo, is a chef. (non-essential — I have one brother)

• ✓ The man who lives next door is a chef. (essential — tells us which man)

4. Before a coordinating conjunction joining two independent clauses. When and, but, or, so, yet, for, nor join two complete sentences, put a comma before the conjunction.

• ✓ I called twice, but no one answered.

• ✓ She studied hard, so she passed easily.

Do not add a comma when the conjunction simply joins two verbs (not two full clauses).

• ✗ She studied hard, and passed. → ✓ She studied hard and passed.

5. With direct address and dates. Use a comma to set off the name of the person spoken to, and within dates.

• ✓ Thanks, Maria, for your help.

• ✓ Let’s eat, Grandma. (Without the comma — Let’s eat Grandma — the meaning changes alarmingly.)

• ✓ She was born on June 19, 2026, in Berlin. (AmE style; note the comma after the year too)

• ✓ She was born on 19 June 2026 in Berlin. (BrE style usually needs no commas)

⚠️ The Comma Splice — A Common Serious Error A comma splice happens when two complete sentences are joined with only a comma. - ✗ It was late, we went home. You can fix it in one of three ways: 1. Use a full stop: ✓ It was late. We went home. 2. Use a semicolon: ✓ It was late; we went home. 3. Add a coordinating conjunction: ✓ It was late, so we went home. Note: however, therefore, then, and moreover are not coordinating conjunctions, so a comma before them still creates a splice. Use a semicolon: ✓ It was late; however, we stayed.

The Semicolon and the Colon

The semicolon (;) links two closely related independent clauses without a conjunction. Each side could stand alone as a sentence.

• ✓ The roads were icy; the buses stopped running.

• ✓ Some people love winter; others can’t wait for spring.

It also separates list items that already contain commas.

• ✓ The tour visits Paris, France; Rome, Italy; and Madrid, Spain.

The colon (:) introduces something: a list, an explanation, or an example. What comes before a colon should normally be a complete clause.

• ✓ She had one goal: to finish the marathon.

• ✓ Bring three things: a pen, paper, and an open mind.

• ✗ Bring: a pen, paper, and an open mind. (the part before the colon is not a full clause)

Mark · Use it to… · Example
▸ Semicolon
   Use it to…: Join two related complete sentences
   Example: I was tired; I kept working.
▸ Colon
   Use it to…: Introduce a list, explanation, or result
   Example: I had one wish: rest.

The Apostrophe

The apostrophe has two main jobs: showing contractions and showing possession.

Contractions — the apostrophe marks missing letters.

• ✓ do not → don’t, I am → I’m, they will → they’ll, of the clock → o’clock

Possession — add ’s to singular nouns, and just an ‘ to plural nouns already ending in -s.

Case · Rule · Example
▸ Singular
   Rule: add ’s
   Example: the girl’s bag
▸ Singular ending in -s
   Rule: usually add ’s
   Example: James’s car (BrE often James’)
▸ Plural ending in -s
   Rule: add ‘ only
   Example: the girls’ bags
▸ Irregular plural
   Rule: add ’s
   Example: the children’s toys, women’s rights

⚠️ Its vs It’s, and Decades - it’s = it is or it has: ✓ It’s raining. / It’s been a long day. - its = belonging to it (no apostrophe):

✓ The dog wagged its tail. - ✗ Its raining. / ✗ The dog wagged it’s tail. - Decades take no apostrophe: ✓ the 1990s, the 80s — ✗ the 1990’s, the 80’s. - Never use an apostrophe to make an ordinary plural: ✗ apple’s for sale → ✓ apples for sale.

Quotation Marks

Quotation marks enclose direct speech and quoted words.

• ✓ “I’ll be there at six,” she said.

BrE vs AmE — quotation marks: - AmE typically uses double quotation marks first: He said, “Hello.” - BrE often uses single quotation marks first: He said, ‘Hello.’ - Quotes inside quotes switch to the other style: AmE “She said ‘no’ twice.” / BrE ‘She said “no” twice.’

The bigger difference is where the final period or comma goes.

• AmE: the comma/period goes inside the closing quotation mark.

• ✓ He called it “brilliant.”

• BrE: the comma/period usually goes outside (unless it belongs to the quoted material).

• ✓ He called it ‘brilliant’.

Question marks and exclamation marks go inside only if they belong to the quotation: ✓ She asked, “Are you ready?” but ✓ Did he really say “no”?

Hyphen vs Dash

The hyphen (-) is short. It joins words, especially compound modifiers before a noun, and links some prefixes.

• ✓ a well-known author, a five-year-old child, a part-time job

• Note: do not hyphenate when the words come after the noun: ✓ The author is well known.

A dash is longer and separates, rather than joins.

• The en dash (–) marks ranges: ✓ pages 10–20, the 2010–2020 period.

• The em dash (—) marks a strong break or aside: ✓ She paused — just for a moment — and smiled.

Tip: A hyphen joins; a dash interrupts. They are different lengths and different jobs.

Parentheses

Parentheses ( ) — called round brackets in BrE — enclose extra, non-essential information. The sentence should still read correctly if you remove them.

• ✓ The museum (founded in 1880) is free on Sundays.

• ✓ Call me later (after lunch is best).

Punctuation belonging to the whole sentence goes outside the closing parenthesis: ✓ We met in Rome (in spring).

Capitalization

Capitalize the following:

Capitalize · Example
▸ The first word of a sentence — ✓ The sun rose.
▸ The pronoun I — ✓ Yesterday I left early.
▸ People’s names — ✓ Anna Smith
▸ Places — ✓ Paris, the Nile, Asia
▸ Nationalities, languages — ✓ Spanish food, she speaks Arabic

Capitalize · Example
▸ Days and months — ✓ Monday, October
▸ Titles of works (main words) — ✓ The Lord of the Rings
▸ Titles before a name — ✓ President Lincoln, Doctor Patel
▸ Holidays, brands, organizations — ✓ Ramadan, Sony, the United Nations

Do not capitalize:

• Seasons: ✗ I love Summer. → ✓ I love summer.

• General directions: ✓ Drive south for an hour. (but capitalize regions: ✓ the South of the country)

• Titles used generally: ✓ She wants to be a doctor. (vs ✓ Doctor Patel)

• Common nouns after a brand or place: ✓ French fries but

✓ a french press is often lowercased; ✓ English grammar (language stays capitalized).

• ✓ On Tuesday, I met a French teacher in March.

• ✗ on tuesday, i met a french Teacher in march.

Part B — Common Mistakes & Confused Pairs

This section is a quick reference. For each pair, you get the confusion, the rule, and a ✓ /✗ example.

Confused Word Pairs

Words · Rule · Example
▸ its / it’s
   Rule: its = possessive; it’s = it is/ has
   Example: ✓ It’s lost its shine.

Words · Rule · Example
▸ your / you’re
   Rule: your = possessive; you’re = you are
   Example: ✓ You’re losing your keys.
▸ their / there / they’re
   Rule: possession / place / they are
   Example: ✓ They’re putting their bags over there.
▸ whose / who’s
   Rule: whose = possessive; who’s = who is/has
   Example: ✓ Who’s the man whose car is blocked?
▸ to / too / two
   Rule: direction-or-infinitive / also-or-excess / the number 2
   Example: ✓ I want to go too, with my two friends.
▸ then / than
   Rule: then = time; than = comparison
   Example: ✓ She’s taller than me; back then she was shorter.
▸ affect / effect
   Rule: affect = verb (to influence); effect = noun (a result)
   Example: ✓ The noise affected me; it had a real effect.
▸ fewer / less
   Rule: fewer = countable; less = uncountable
   Example: ✓ Fewer cars, less traffic.
▸ lie / lay
   Rule: lie = recline (no object); lay = put down (needs object)
   Example: ✓ I lie down; I lay the book on the table.
▸ who / whom
   Rule: who = subject; whom = object
   Example: ✓ Who called? / To whom did you speak?
▸ e.g. / i.e.
   Rule: e.g. = for example; i.e. = that is
   Example: ✓ fruit, e.g. apples / ✓ citrus fruit, i.e. lemons and limes
▸ advice / advise
   Rule: advice = noun; advise = verb
   Example: ✓ I advise you to take my advice.
▸ practice / practise
   Rule: BrE: practice = noun, practise = verb (AmE: practice for both)
   Example: ✓ I practise daily. (BrE verb) / ✓ good practice
▸ lose / loose
   Rule: lose = misplace/not win; loose = not tight
   Example: ✓ Don’t lose the loose screw.
▸ accept / except
   Rule: accept = receive; except = apart from
   Example: ✓ Everyone accepted except me.
▸ principal / principle
   Rule: principal = main / head of school; principle = a rule or belief
   Example: ✓ The principal acted on principle.

Words · Rule · Example
▸ stationary / stationery
   Rule: stationary = not moving; stationery = paper goods
   Example: ✓ The van was stationary; I bought stationery.
▸ complement / compliment
   Rule: complement = completes; compliment = praise
   Example: ✓ The wine complements the meal; she paid me a compliment.
▸ everyday / every day
   Rule: everyday = ordinary (adjective); every day = each day
   Example: ✓ an everyday task / ✓ I exercise every day.
▸ into / in to
   Rule: into = movement/transformation; in to = two words
   Example: ✓ She walked into the room. / ✓ He came in to help.

Quick check for who/whom: If you can answer the question with he/she/they, use who. If you’d answer with him/her/them, use whom. ✓ Whom did you see? — I saw him.

Subject–Verb Agreement Traps

These constructions trip up even advanced learners.

Pattern · Rule · Example
▸ everyone / everybody / each / no one
   Rule: always singular
   Example: ✓ Everyone is here. (✗ are)
▸ the number of
   Rule: takes a singular verb
   Example: ✓ The number of students is rising.
▸ a number of
   Rule: takes a plural verb
   Example: ✓ A number of students are absent.
▸ neither / either (alone)
   Rule: singular
   Example: ✓ Neither answer is correct.
▸ neither… nor / either… or
   Rule: verb agrees with the nearer subject
   Example: ✓ Neither the boys nor the teacher was late. / ✓ Neither the teacher nor the boys were late.

Pattern · Rule · Example
▸ collective nouns (team, family, government)
   Rule: AmE usually singular; BrE may use plural
   Example: AmE ✓ The team is winning. / BrE ✓ The team are winning.

Other Frequent Learner Errors

Error · Why it’s wrong · Correction
▸ ✗ I don’t know nothing.
   Why it’s wrong: double negative
   Correction: ✓ I don’t know anything.
▸ ✗ could of / should of / would of
   Why it’s wrong: “of” misheard for “have”
   Correction: ✓ could have, should have, would have
▸ ✗ more better / most easiest
   Why it’s wrong: double comparative/ superlative
   Correction: ✓ better, easiest
▸ ✗ very unique / quite perfect
   Why it’s wrong: unique and perfect are absolutes
   Correction: ✓ unique, perfect (or almost unique)
▸ ✗ apple’s for sale
   Why it’s wrong: apostrophe on a plain plural
   Correction: ✓ apples for sale
▸ ✗ I can’t hardly see.
   Why it’s wrong: hardly is already negative
   Correction: ✓ I can hardly see.

⚠️ The “could of” trap: In speech, could have sounds like could of (the contraction is could’ve). In writing, always use have: ✓ You could have told me. — ✗ You could of told me.

Quick Review

• End statements with a full stop/period, questions with a question mark, and strong feeling with a single exclamation mark.

• The comma separates list items, follows introductory elements, brackets non-essential information, and precedes a coordinating conjunction joining two clauses.

• A comma splice joins two sentences with only a comma — fix it with a full stop, a semicolon, or a conjunction.

• The semicolon links related independent clauses; the colon introduces a list, explanation, or result.

• The apostrophe marks contractions and possession — but its is possessive, it’s means it is, and decades (1990s) take no apostrophe.

• Quotation marks: AmE prefers double and puts commas/periods inside; BrE often prefers single and puts them outside.

• A hyphen joins (compound modifiers); a dash interrupts; the en dash marks ranges.

• Capitalize sentence starts, I, proper nouns, nationalities, languages, days, months, and titles — but not seasons.

• Watch the confused pairs (your/you’re, their/there/they’re, affect/effect, fewer/less) and avoid could of, double negatives, and very unique.

Practice

Correct the punctuation, capitalization, or word-choice error in each sentence.

1. Its been raining all day, and the streets are flooded.

2. We invited two clowns, a magician and a juggler.

3. The meeting was long we left early.

4. My sister who is a doctor lives in canada.

5. You should of called me yesterday.

6. There going to bring they’re books to the library over their.

7. I love the cold weather in Winter.

8. Less people came to the second show than to the first.

9. Each of the students have submitted their essay.

10. James asked, “where are you going”?

Answers

1. ✓ It’s been raining all day, and the streets are flooded. (it’s = it has)

2. ✓ We invited two clowns, a magician, and a juggler. (serial/Oxford comma clarifies separate acts; in BrE the comma is optional but helpful here)

3. ✓ The meeting was long, so we left early. (comma splice fixed — also valid: …long; we left early. or …long. We left early.)

4. ✓ My sister, who is a doctor, lives in Canada. (non-essential clause needs commas; Canada is a proper noun)

5. ✓ You should have called me yesterday. (should of → should have)

6. ✓ They’re going to bring their books to the library over there. (they are / possessive / place)

7. ✓ I love the cold weather in winter. (seasons are not capitalized)

8. ✓ Fewer people came to the second show than to the first. (people is countable → fewer)

9. ✓ Each of the students has submitted his or her essay. (each is singular → has; their is widely accepted, but the verb must be has)

10. ✓ James asked, “Where are you going?” (capital after the quotation opens; the question mark belongs to the quotation, so it goes inside, in both AmE and BrE)

blocks.text: ⚠️ The Comma Splice — A Common Serious Error A comma splice happens when two complete sentences are joined with only a comma. - ✗ It was late, we went home. You can fix it in one of three ways: 1. Use a full stop: ✓ It was late. We went home. 2. Use a semicolon: ✓ It was late; we went home. 3. Add a coordinating conjunction: ✓ It was late, so we went home. Note: however, therefore, then, and moreover are not coordinating conjunctions, so a comma before them still creates a splice. Use a semicolon: ✓ It was late; however, we stayed.

blocks.text: Confused Word Pairs
blocks.html: Confused Word Pairs

blocks.text:
Words · Rule · Example
▸ its / it’s
   Rule: its = possessive; it’s = it is/ has
   Example: ✓ It’s lost its shine.
blocks.html: Words · Rule · Example ▸ its / it’s Rule: its = possessive; it’s = it is/ has Example: ✓ It’s lost its shine.

blocks.text:
Words · Rule · Example
▸ your / you’re
   Rule: your = possessive; you’re = you are
   Example: ✓ You’re losing your keys.
▸ their / there / they’re
   Rule: possession / place / they are
   Example: ✓ They’re putting their bags over there.
▸ whose / who’s
   Rule: whose = possessive; who’s = who is/has
   Example: ✓ Who’s the man whose car is blocked?
▸ to / too / two
   Rule: direction-or-infinitive / also-or-excess / the number 2
   Example: ✓ I want to go too, with my two friends.
▸ then / than
   Rule: then = time; than = comparison
   Example: ✓ She’s taller than me; back then she was shorter.
▸ affect / effect
   Rule: affect = verb (to influence); effect = noun (a result)
   Example: ✓ The noise affected me; it had a real effect.
▸ fewer / less
   Rule: fewer = countable; less = uncountable
   Example: ✓ Fewer cars, less traffic.
▸ lie / lay
   Rule: lie = recline (no object); lay = put down (needs object)
   Example: ✓ I lie down; I lay the book on the table.
▸ who / whom
   Rule: who = subject; whom = object
   Example: ✓ Who called? / To whom did you speak?
▸ e.g. / i.e.
   Rule: e.g. = for example; i.e. = that is
   Example: ✓ fruit, e.g. apples / ✓ citrus fruit, i.e. lemons and limes
▸ advice / advise
   Rule: advice = noun; advise = verb
   Example: ✓ I advise you to take my advice.
▸ practice / practise
   Rule: BrE: practice = noun, practise = verb (AmE: practice for both)
   Example: ✓ I practise daily. (BrE verb) / ✓ good practice
▸ lose / loose
   Rule: lose = misplace/not win; loose = not tight
   Example: ✓ Don’t lose the loose screw.
▸ accept / except
   Rule: accept = receive; except = apart from
   Example: ✓ Everyone accepted except me.
▸ principal / principle
   Rule: principal = main / head of school; principle = a rule or belief
   Example: ✓ The principal acted on principle.

glossary.def: The form of a sentence in which the subject performs the action of the verb; it contrasts with the passive voice. The dog chased the cat.
A word that describes or modifies a noun or pronoun, giving information about qualities such as size, colour, or number. a tall building.
A word that modifies a verb, an adjective, another adverb, or a whole sentence, often expressing manner, place, time, frequency, or degree. Many end in -ly. She sang beautifully.
A word, phrase, or clause that functions the way an adverb does, adding information about how, when, where, or why. He left in a hurry.
The matching of grammatical forms so that related words share features such as number and person, most often a verb agreeing with its subject. She walks; they walk.
The noun or noun phrase that a pronoun refers back to. Maria lost her keys, but she found them later. (Maria is the antecedent of she.)
The punctuation mark (’) used to show possession or to mark omitted letters in a contraction. the dog’s bone; don’t.
A word placed before a noun to show whether it is specific or general. English has the definite article the and the indefinite articles a and an. See also zero article.

The grammatical category that shows how an action relates to the flow of time, such as whether it is in progress or completed. English has two main aspects, the continuous (progressive) and the perfect. She is reading; she has read.
A “helping” verb used with a main verb to form tenses, questions, negatives, or the passive. The primary auxiliaries are be, do, and have. She is working; do you know? See also modal verb.
The infinitive used without the word to, appearing after modal verbs and certain other verbs. You should go; let me help.

A group of words containing a subject and a finite verb. A main (independent) clause can stand alone; a subordinate (dependent) clause cannot and depends on a main clause. I stayed home because it was raining.
A noun that refers to a group of people or things as a single unit: team, family, committee, flock. It can take a singular or plural verb depending on the meaning.
The form of an adjective or adverb used to compare two things, formed with -er or more. taller, more carefully. See also superlative.
A word or phrase that completes the meaning of a verb, often describing the subject or object. She is a doctor; the soup tastes delicious.
A noun made up of two or more words acting as a single unit. toothbrush, swimming pool, mother-in-law.
A structure (often using if) that expresses that one thing depends on another, describing possible or imagined situations. If it rains, we will stay in.
The verb aspect formed with be + the -ing participle, showing an action in progress. They are watching television.
A shortened form in which two words are combined and missing letters are marked by an apostrophe. don’t (do not), she’s (she is), we’ll (we will).
A conjunction that joins words, phrases, or clauses of equal grammatical rank: and, but, or, nor, for, so, yet. I tried, but I failed.
A noun naming something that can be counted and that has both singular and plural forms. one book, two books. Contrast with uncountable noun.
A modifying phrase that does not logically attach to the word it is meant to describe, often because that word is missing. Walking to school, the rain began to fall. (The rain was not walking.)
The word the, used before a noun to refer to something specific or already known. Please pass the salt.
A word that points to something and shows whether it is near or far: this, that, these, those. This* is mine; those* are yours.
Another name for a subordinate clause: a clause that cannot stand alone and relies on a main clause. …although she was tired.
A word placed before a noun to identify or quantify it, such as an article, demonstrative, possessive, or quantifier. the, this, my, some, every.
The noun or pronoun that receives the action of a transitive verb. She read a book.
Reporting words by quoting them exactly, usually within quotation marks. He said, “I am leaving now.” Contrast with indirect (reported) speech.
The omission of words that can be understood from the context. She can sing and (she can) dance. The term also names the punctuation mark (…) that shows omitted text.
A verb form that shows tense, person, and number and can serve as the main verb of a clause. She writes; they wrote. Contrast with non-finite forms (infinitives, participles).
The category showing who is involved: the first person is the speaker (I, we), the second person the listener (you), and the third person the one spoken about (he, she, it, they).
The -ing form of a verb used as a noun. Swimming* is good exercise; I enjoy reading*.

An adjective describing a quality that can exist in different degrees, so it can be used with words like very or in comparative forms. cold, colder, very cold. Contrast with non-gradable adjectives like perfect.
The verb form used to give commands, instructions, or requests, usually with no stated subject. Close* the door; be* careful.
The words a and an, used before a singular countable noun to refer to something non-specific. I saw a dog and an owl.
A clause containing a subject and a finite verb that can stand alone as a complete sentence; also called a main clause. The sun rose.
The person or thing that receives the direct object, often answering “to whom?” or “for whom?”. She gave him a gift.
Reporting what someone said without quoting the exact words, usually with changes to tense and pronouns. He said (that) he was leaving. Contrast with direct speech.
The base form of a verb, usually preceded by to. I want to learn. See also bare infinitive.
A change in the form of a word to express grammatical meaning such as tense, number, or comparison. walk → walked; cat → cats.
A verb that does not take a direct object. She slept. Contrast with transitive verb.
A verb that does not form its past tense and past participle with the regular -ed ending. go → went → gone.
A verb that connects the subject to a complement that describes or identifies it, rather than showing an action: be, seem, become, appear, feel. He seems tired.
The verb in a clause that carries the principal meaning, as opposed to an auxiliary. She has finished. (Finished is the main verb; has is the auxiliary.)
An auxiliary verb expressing meanings such as ability, possibility, permission, obligation, or advice: can, could, may, might, must, shall, should, will, would. You must wait; she can swim.
A word or group of words that describes or limits another element in a sentence. Adjectives and adverbs are common modifiers. a bright light.

The grammatical category that shows the speaker’s attitude toward what is said: stating a fact (indicative), giving a command (imperative), or expressing a wish or hypothesis (subjunctive). He goes; Go!; I wish he were here.
A word, form, or structure that expresses denial or absence, typically using not or words like no, never, nobody. She does not know.
A relative clause that adds extra, non-essential information about a noun and is set off by commas; removing it does not change the basic meaning. My brother, who lives in Rome, is a chef.
A word that names a person, place, thing, idea, or quality. teacher, London, table, freedom.
A noun together with the words that modify it, functioning as a single unit in a sentence. the tall man in the grey coat.
A noun, pronoun, or noun phrase affected by the action of a verb or governed by a preposition. It may be a direct object, an indirect object, or the object of a preposition. She kicked the ball.
A verb form used in compound tenses, in the passive, or as an adjective. The present participle ends in -ing (running); the past participle usually ends in -ed or is irregular (walked, broken).
A short word, often resembling a preposition or adverb, that combines with a verb to form a phrasal verb. give up, look after, turn off.
The form in which the subject receives the action rather than performing it, formed with be + past participle. The cat was chased by the dog. Contrast with active voice.
The verb form used to refer to actions or states in the past. She walked home; they were happy.
The verb aspect formed with have + past participle, linking an earlier action to a later point in time. I have finished.
A verb combined with one or more particles whose meaning often differs from the separate words. give up (stop), look after (care for), put off (postpone).
A group of words working together as a unit but, unlike a clause, not containing both a subject and a finite verb. in the morning; the old house.
The grammatical form indicating more than one. books, children, women. Contrast with singular.
A form showing ownership or a close relationship, made with an apostrophe and s or with a possessive word. Tom’s car; my, your, mine, hers.
The part of a clause that says something about the subject, containing the verb and any objects, complements, or adverbials. The children played in the garden.
A group of letters added to the beginning of a word to change its meaning. un-happy, re-write. See also suffix.
A word that shows the relationship of a noun or pronoun to another word, often expressing position, direction, or time: in, on, at, under, before, between. The cat is under the table.
A preposition together with its object and any modifiers, working as a unit. on the table; after a long day; in the morning.
The verb form used to refer to current actions, habits, general truths, or states. She works here; water boils at 100°C.
A word used in place of a noun or noun phrase to avoid repetition: I, you, he, she, it, they, who, this, mine. Maria called and she sounded happy.
A noun naming a particular person, place, or organisation, normally written with a capital letter. London, Sarah, Microsoft, Monday.
A determiner or phrase expressing quantity without an exact number: some, many, much, few, several, a lot of. Many people came.
A short question added to the end of a statement, usually to invite agreement or confirmation. You’re coming, aren’t you? She didn’t call, did she?
A pronoun ending in -self or -selves that refers back to the subject: myself, yourself, himself, themselves. She taught herself to paint.
The level of formality and style of language chosen to suit a situation, audience, or purpose. Formal: “I would be grateful if you could…”; informal: “Can you…?”
A verb that forms its past tense and past participle by adding -ed to the base form. walk → walked. Contrast with irregular verb.
A clause that gives more information about a noun, usually introduced by a relative pronoun. The man who lives next door is a doctor. See also non-defining relative clause.
A pronoun that introduces a relative clause and refers back to a noun: who, whom, whose, which, that. the book that I read.
Another name for indirect speech: reporting what was said without quoting the exact words. She said she was tired.
A complete unit of meaning containing at least one main clause, beginning with a capital letter and ending with a full stop, question mark, or exclamation mark. The bell rang.
The grammatical form indicating just one. book, child, woman. Contrast with plural.
A verb that describes a state or condition rather than an action, and is not usually used in the continuous form: know, believe, own, like, seem. I know the answer (not I am knowing).
The person or thing that performs the action of the verb or about which the sentence makes a statement. The children are playing.
A verb mood expressing wishes, suggestions, demands, or hypothetical situations, often with a base-form verb or were. I suggest that he be present.
A clause that cannot stand alone and depends on a main clause, usually introduced by a subordinating conjunction or relative pronoun; also called a dependent clause. We left after the film ended.
A conjunction that introduces a subordinate clause and links it to a main clause: because, although, if, when, while, since, unless. Call me when you arrive.
A group of letters added to the end of a word to change its meaning or part of speech. happi-ness, quick-ly. See also prefix.
The form of an adjective or adverb used to compare three or more things and show the highest degree, formed with -est or most. the tallest. See also comparative.
A unit of pronunciation containing one vowel sound, with or without surrounding consonants. cat has one syllable; wa- ter has two; ba-na-na has three.
The form of a verb that shows the time of an action or state, chiefly present or past, and combined with aspect to express finer time relationships. She plays; she played.
A verb that takes a direct object to complete its meaning. She wrote a letter. Contrast with intransitive verb.
A noun naming something that cannot normally be counted and has no plural form, such as a substance or abstract idea: water, information, advice, furniture. I need some advice (not an advice).
A word that expresses an action, an event, or a state of being. run, think, become, exist. They ran to the bus.
The grammatical category showing whether the subject performs the action (active voice) or receives it (passive voice). The chef cooked the meal / The meal was cooked.
A category into which words are grouped according to how they behave in a sentence: noun, verb, adjective, adverb, pronoun, preposition, conjunction, determiner, and interjection.
The absence of any article before a noun, common with plural and uncountable nouns used in a general sense. I like music; cats are independent.
